item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I have to admit — I didn't really get this one until I read through the comments. So, it's a Mars rover that's gone sightseeing, and the "tourist attractions" it's visiting are different things related to Mars on a conceptual level? Altogether, it's a neat concept. It's quirky, it's weird in all the right ways. The build-up is enjoyable. A lot here is well-written — it's clear the author(s)1 knew exactly what they were doing, and that's respectable.

I guess my issue is that it takes a premise, builds up toward it, and then… Doesn't do much else? I mean, the Addendum was neat, but I thought it overstayed its welcome. I thought it had lost its lustre before I even reached the table's halfway point. I was also disappointed by the restrictions put on the images (most are too small and of too low a quality), but I think I understand why that was done. It's to hide the fact that these are otherwise regular, real-world images, where nothing anomalous is happening?

Overall, I need to give this one a rare no-vote because, while I enjoyed the premise immensely, I think this is missing something. But there's not enough here to dislike — the parts that are good are really competent.

Footnotes
1. Someone else semi-rewrote this?

item.title: A Wanderer and Voyager, Worthy of the SCP
item.content:encoded:
I’ve already voted, but I’d thought that I would add that it should have a story of it accidentally voyaging into Foundation sites (including the Moonbase) and Foundation personnel noticing it, chasing it like a chicken. If it did wander into Foundation sites, where else would it wander. To a Fifthist Church Meeting? Where the Flesh That Hates reside? Would it wander into the GOC? Would the UIU report it as an odd meeting?

The possibilities of this thing should make it more possible for a Foundation droid. Exploring where no drone has gone before.

item.title: Direction!
item.content:encoded:
…is what IMHO this article lacks. Now 206 is a rover which works even though it should not. Now it is a teleporter. Now it can also travel in time and to parallel universes. Now it seems to be sentient, crying over its creator's grave. Now in turn it has taken to threatening researchers as well as has somehow learned to print its pictures… Each of these individual bits (with the exception of the interview, which is awful) works for me. As a whole, they feel like a mess.

Furthermore, 206 feels a bit like a VGER rip-off… which, however is not necessarily a bad thing.

item.content:encoded:
The Russian site has stuff that we don't, and can be translated over to here? Well, that explains the various odd wordings in this anyway…

My main problem with this is that there doesn't seem to be anything saying that this Invictus probe is actually SCP-206. They can't see it in the photos, it's doing things a rover can't do, they don't even know where it is (which is kind of a red flag) so what's to say the effect has anything to do Invictus at all? The SCP should really be identified as the photos, I think. No doubt tied to the Invictus mission, of course, since that's when it started, I just feel a disconnect between "rover we lost contact with" and "pictures from impossible angles all over the solar system and other dimensions". Maybe it's just me.

EDIT: This is literally the stupidest comment I've ever left on this site. This thing is great! The worst part of it is inconsistency in the writing of the addenda, but that's it.

item.title: This is facking terrible.
item.content:encoded:
1. It's either safe or euclid, make up your mind.

2. No idea where it is, and no procedures to contain it - it's not an SCP.

I hope this article burns to the ground.

Another thing; if wideband radio jamming was executed on a global scale of an intensity to block detection by radio telescopes and local receivers (which would be required to block a signal from space) you'd have outages of almost all radio communications.
